ECE 6390 / Digital signals

Multipath and OFDM

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how one echo creates frequency-dependent fading, and why a cyclic prefix can simplify a multicarrier receiver.

A direct path plus a delayed echo has H(f) = 1 + a exp(−j2πfτ), where a is the echo voltage ratio and τ is delay. The paths reinforce at some frequencies and cancel at others. This is a frequency-selective channel.

OFDM divides the useful symbol into orthogonal subcarriers spaced Δf = 1/Tu. With a long enough cyclic prefix and correct timing, channel convolution over the useful interval becomes circular. Each subcarrier then sees a complex gain that a receiver can estimate and equalize.

The prefix costs transmission time. A longer useful interval reduces its fractional overhead but increases sensitivity to time variation and frequency offset. Deep spectral fades also remain difficult because equalization can amplify noise.

Example

For τ = 1 µs and equal path amplitudes, the first cancellation occurs at f = 0.5 MHz. Subcarrier spacing 100 kHz gives Tu = 10 µs. A 1.2 µs prefix exceeds this delay in the ideal two-path timing model and occupies about 10.7% of the total symbol interval.

    Practice

    1. What useful-symbol duration corresponds to 50 kHz subcarrier spacing?

    Use Tu = 1/Δf and keep seconds and hertz consistent.

    Tu = 1/(50,000 Hz) = 20 µs.

    2. Does a prefix longer than the echo delay eliminate a deep frequency-domain channel null?

    Separate circular-convolution structure from the value of H(f).

    It prevents adjacent useful-symbol interference under the ideal assumptions and enables one-tap subcarrier equalization. A channel null remains a weak or lost subcarrier and can severely amplify equalized noise.
